rv.q: Drood, ultimately, is not a complete show so much as an expandable playspace, and with performers of this caliber, an evening of yeasty, nudge-nudge-wink-wink British good humor is more or less guaranteed.
All in all, Ellis has stars, zest and stellar escapist material on his side.
The musical “Edwin Drood” at least leaves behind moments of shimmering musical pleasure to savor, long after the miscreant of the night has been booed off the stage.
It's a fine production, considering how tricky the piece is.

"The Mystery of Edwin Drood" ran for 608 performances. Now the Roundabout Theatre Company has brought "Drood" back to Broadway in a revival directed with rip-roaring éclat by Scott Ellis, and I'll be surprised if it doesn't run at least as long as the original 1985 production. For sheer fun, this show is hard to top.
Director Scott Ellis, a Roundabout fixture since 1993, turns in his best musical outing in memory.

Perhaps the best part is watching the first-rate cast have so much fun — Stephanie J. Block shows real comedic power, Jim Norton is having a ball, Chita Rivera is giggly, Gregg Edelman is just silly and Will Chase is over-acting perfectly...
Instead of trusting the characters and the mystery to build the suspense, however, Holmes aims for the campy, tiresome and childish.
But regardless of the accomplished cast and sparkling design and direction in Roundabout's Broadway revival, nothing great can come of mediocre material.
It most exactly suggests the experience of seeing Rupert Holmes' musical, a production that embraces its audience in distinctively enjoyable ways.
"The Mystery of Edwin Drood," inspired by an unfinished Charles Dickens novel, is one of the most inventive, inspired and rousing musicals ever devised.
It’s inordinately fun to vote in a low-stakes election for a change.
Suspiciously, I have to wonder if this is one entertainment that is just more fun to perform than to watch.
Its use of pantomime, the iconography of gestures, the baseness of humor, and constant winking at the audience are really over the top.
Alas, the show still makes my teeth hurt.
“Drood” is clever, smart, entertaining and the best musical revival of the New York season.

cn.t: Critics find this boisterous revival of Holmes' interactive musical a fun, well-cast crowd-pleaser, though some dismiss the material as thin and one-note despite the game ensemble's spirited efforts.

sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Orchestra rows E-G as the best seats overall, citing 'a winning mix of perfect proximity and elevated view over the heads in front' on a good rake with a low stage. Headout notes the 'outstanding inclination' keeps sightlines clear from middle rows. AVFMS Row D seat 2: 'Perfect view with unlimited legroom.' 16-row section seats ~350 of the 413 total; low stage means front rows don't require neck strain.

SeatPlan explicitly names Left and Right Mezzanine as 'the best value seats at the Laura Pels Theatre,' citing cheap tickets vs. central Orchestra with 'a clear and close view.' Only 3 rows (AA/BB/CC), under 100 seats — feels intimate and close to stage. Headout confirms 'very little restriction from the Mezzanine overhang at the back' of the Orchestra, meaning the Mezzanine itself is close/low. Row BB flagged by Headout as a specific value row.
